PRO-TYPISTS, INC.

PROCEEDINGS

I'm with my dear friend of long years, standing friendhip, association, Mr. Teddy Wilson - and we're doing a tape for the Jazz Oral History (Project) for the Smithsonian Institute, and this is about Teddy's life, and we'd like for this to be his way, the way he wants to tell it.
Teddy, how you doing?
Just fine, Milt.
Good.
So glad you contacted me to do this history.
Thank you.

So I guess that a good place to start would be back to my earliest recollections as a child back in Austin, Texas. I was born in Austin, Texas on November 24, 1912, and my father's name was James Augustus Wilson, my mother was Pearl Georgia Shaw, her maiden name.
When I was born, I had one older brother, a year and a half older than me, James Augustus, Jr., after my father -- we call him Gus. His nickname was always Gus for Augustus.
Right.
And the first recollections, like maybe

when I was four or five years old in Austin, Texas, where my father and mother were both on the faculty of the Sam Houston College, which in those days, was right there in Austin, and which later merged with the Tillotson School, I guess.
Uh huh.
In those days, it was Sam Houston College, and I remember my very, very early schooling there ... learning to read and write --
What did your mother and father teach? The subjects.

My father was the Dean there, the Dean of Men, I believe his job was -- and my mother taught in the elementary grades, and she taught my brother, Gus -- and me, to read and write at home, so we actually entered school in the second grade when we were about four years old, because she had taught us all that material, and in the south, in those days, there was nothing compulsory about having to be six years old to go in the first grade.
Right.
So we went right in the fourth grade; I was four and my brother was five at Sam Houston there.
And then my father got a better job at Tuskegee Institute under Booker T. Washington -- and I guess that
would have been maybe around 1915 or '16, something like that, and then the whole family had moved to Alabama.*
What town in Alabama?
Tuskegee.
Oh, Tuskegee.
Yeah, Tuskegee, the Tuskegee Institute, and the third part of Tuskegee was a big VA hospital, but that came later after the first world war.

Tell me this, Teddy -- it's quite unusual, I mean, I'm from the south, and your parents were both professors in education. They were much ahead of their time for that era, of black people having this kind of an educational background, isn't that right?

That is true. My father was. My mother, at that time, when I was born, she had a high school education. She had gone to what we called State Normal or the other name for it was Alabama State in Montgomery, Alabama.

But my father had come south from the north. He had graduated with honors from Wesleyan University in Middletown, Connecticut, in the graduating class of 1907, and incidentally, I have -- as a very nice gift, it was given to me a few years ago; I was playing at the Sheraton Tobacco Valley Inn on Route 91, just north of Hartford, and some of the students from Wesleyan made me
*Washington died in 1915.

a surprise present of xerox pages from the yearbook of 1907 with my father's picture in it, and his whole -- you know, the paragraphs they put in there, the honors he won that year, and who gave him his degree and so on, like that.

So that's a very prize possession I have. If these students hadn't made me a surprise gift of that, I would never have had, you know, except hearsay from my relatives, that my father went to that school. But I do actually have photostat pictures of him and two of his classmates on the same page.

Incidentally, before I go any further, the interesting side light, is that in those days, I remember clearly -- the tuition and the room and board for one man -- two in a room -- but one man, was only $163 a year. That's in a college, now.
Oh, my goodness.
That was for a college education, room and board, and two men in a room -- $163. That's a long time passed, isn't it?

I'm telling you; that's amazing. It's interesting to hear that. And that's just so good, Teddy. Now about your parents -- before I interject this, you were in Tuskegee and your parents had gotten to Tuskegee. Now go on from there.
Yes, they'd left Texas to go to
Alabama, and my father got this job at Tuskegee Institute -- and Booker T. Washington was still President and founder of that school in Tuskegee.

But then my mother didn't have a job there, and until he could get her on the faculty there, she took me and my brother, Gus, and we lived a little while at my grandparents' home in Montgomery, Alabama, and went to the elementary school of Alabama State for awhile. And then later on, my father got my mother a job teaching elementary adult classes in Tuskegee, and then we all --she moved, and rejoined my father there in a house that was part of his job at that time, for the whole family. So we were residents of the residential community called Greenwood, outside of -- just on the edge of the campus.
So that was home and schooling, and my father and mother's job all in one -- and my brother and I went right on up through that school on through high school.
That's great. Now which grandparents were these, Teddy?
These are my mother's parents in Montgomery. I have no knowledge of my father's parents, except that --
What were their names, Teddy?
Shaw was that family name.
Uh huh. Your grandfather on your
mother's side was -- Shaw.
But do you remember his first name?

I don't know -- everybody used to just call him 'Grandpa Shaw' or Papa Shaw; I mean, we're going back to when I was only 5 or 6 years old. See, he died -- oh, I remember, at that time he was in his seventies, when I first saw him coming from Texas.

But I really can't remember his first name. But my grandfather was a preacher and a barber, I believe, was his work over the years, and he had a big family -- my mother came from a large family. There were six -- evenly divided -- six girls and six boys in the family, and they've all passed on now in 1979, except for three of the girls [who] are still alive. My mother has passed away, but the three youngest sisters are still alive, and the three older have died, and all six of the men in the family died.
Uh huh.
So you went through school in Montgomery -- is that right?

No. Just a short period of schooling in Montgomery -- between Texas and Tuskegee, until my father could arrange to get my mother on the staff of Tuskegee, teaching there, we lived at her parents' home in Montgomery, and temporarily went to the elementary school
at Alabama State, which had an elementary department in those days, with little kids.
Uh huh. And where did you go when you were in elementary and high school; I mean, what towns would you be in?

Well, that would be when I got to Tuskegee. So I got a little elementary schooling in Austin, Texas, and then a little in Montgomery -- and then by the time we got to Tuskegee, I think I entered officially the third grade, I believe it would be, in Tuskegee.
Uh huh, I see.

My brother and I were both in the third grade by the time my father got the whole family settled in Tuskegee which was to be, spend the remainder of his life and also my mother's life, in Tuskegee. Both of them are buried right on the campus -- in the graveyard on the campus of Tuskegee right now.
Uh huh.
So they spent the rest of their lives at Tuskegee, from those days.
Did your mother ever teach in Tennessee?
No -- but my mother was born in Tennessee.
Oh, I see.

I think she was born in either Cumberland, Tennessee or in Cumberland County or something like that. I never really tracked that down too much. But it was Tennessee. My father was born in Pennsylvania.
Uh huh. I have some recollections of meeting your mother when I was with Cab Calloway's band in the early days. We were playing there during the time your folks were in Tuskegee.

Well, that very well could have been -- because during the second world war, there was a man named [Bulls] who had a nightclub off campus there at Tuskegee, and he brought many of the big bands who were traveling, who would play there in Tuskegee. I know that Duke Ellington played there, and Cab -- and that's when you probably met my mother.
That's right, I remember that.
Because I know that she got to meet a lot of the musicians.
That's right.
Because so many of the guys in the band were old friends of mine, and when they went to Tuskegee, they met my mother there.
Was George Washington Carver there at Tuskegee at that time?
Oh yes, I remember him very well. Yeah.
What kind of a man was he, Teddy?
He was a very quiet, pleasant man.
Oh, I remember him, too.
He was in his laboratory in the agricultural building, and always doing his experiments and his work in advanced chemistry.
Yeah, with those little tin cans and that.

Yes, sir -- all of his own equipment. He did marvelous things with natural science and chemistry, and I always remember he always made chapel exercises on Sunday, and he would always wear this white flower in his lapel; always a fresh white flower in his lapel.

And the story around the campus -- everybody loved him, but to the people there, you know, they didn't understand him, really, this advanced chemistry, so he was sort of secluded, yes. He was very different than the average faculty member, the people, the community in those days -- advanced scientist as he was, he couldn't talk that stuff with those people.
Oh, sure.
But they all loved him, and everybody was very proud of him and because we all knew, and the whole school knew that these giant corporations in the north had
always tried to get him to join their staffs, and do research and chemistry -- everyone knew how highly he was regarded by the federal government, and the intelligentsia of the northern universities.

Another thing comes to mind about Tuskegee that might be of interest to some people -- Tuskegee was quite a school sports, especially football. The baseball was not outstanding, but the Tuskegee football team went for, oh, five years undefeated. I remember one period there in the twenties, largely due to a man named Benjamin Stevenson, his name was. They called him Steve, which was his nickname, and he was one of the most marvelous football players of the day, and of course, the local people like to compare him with the outstanding white football player of Notre Dame, Red Grange -- he's a big name, at least, but down in Tuskegee, Steve could run as good as Red Grange, and it was very common for Benjamin Stevenson to run from kickoff to touchdown -- that was a very usual occurrence for this man.
And he was a marvelous player -- I remember him.
We had no publicity in those days, too.
What's that?
We had no publicity then.
No, that's right. But oh, Stevenson --
it took more than two men to tackle Stevenson. Fabulous football player.
Uh huh. Did you ever get to know Booker T. Washington to see him or ...
No, by the time my mother and my brother and I had joined my father at Tuskegee, Booker T. Washington had died, and Robert Moten was the new principal.
Uh huh.
So he was the principal while I was there at Tuskegee.
Did you ever hear your mother discuss with either your dad or you any impressions of Mr. Moten, as to what he was like?
You mean, Booker T?
No, Mr. Moten, who took his place.

Oh, Well, I knew Mr. Moten, and he had children of the same age as me and my brother. So we grew up with Moten kids, the younger Moten children -- there were two older and two younger than me and my brother.
Uh huh.

One became a drummer, a musician, and so we were in close contact with those children, but not the Booker T. family. My father was a great admirer of Booker T. -- I think that was one reason he took that job.

He thought Booker T. was a very outstanding man at that time. And you have to remember that Booker T. Washington was born a slave and finally founding a school that is, to this day, one of the leading black colleges of the south.

Of course, times have changed now, you know, since the Supreme Court ordered desegregation of the schools, all of those segregated colleges are in a different position from what they were in those days. But they surely furnished a tremendous -- they filled a tremendous gap in the South. There was Tuskegee, Moorhouse, Atlanta University, and there comes to mind so many of those schools, those segregated schools.
Yeah.
But I do think that Tuskegee, back in those days in the twenties, we were getting education comparable to the northern schools of today in 1979 in a lot of ways.

I'm sure you will share my concern and respect for Booker T. knowing from what he had to come to, that he first had to get us in -- not only an education, but in to finding a job. To be waiters and porters and to know how to work -- and this has been misunderstood down through the years.
Yes, you're right.
And it's very unfortunate, you know,

but this was a basic thing -- first you -- I mean, coming out of slavery without any kind of education or any profession, you had to first learn how to do something, and that I think was what this great man was all about.

That's right. Booker T. Washington installed 22 trades at Tuskegee -- there was a machine shop practice, for making metal parts out of machinery; there was auto mechanics; there was printing, on up to newspaper cylinder press; work on up to job printing, on up to linotype operations, architectural drawing, tailoring, just -- cabinet making, regular carpentry, architecture, as I said, architectural drawing -- and just about everything you could think of, to make a living in a more advanced profession than slavery.
That's right, a proud one.

It was just picking cotton or working out in the fields, or doing domestic work. Slavery was just the lowest -- but these were actual trades. That's what you would call it -- a trade school to equip the person to do the type of work that eventually leads to joining a union and that sort of work, rather than just the lowest level of manual labor. So that was Booker T's...
Right, right.
Now a lot of people, after he started that thing, began to disagree with Booker T. on that, and thought there should be more emphasis on liberal
arts.
But they had to be first this before they could get in academics.
Right -- to get a job.
But there was one serious flaw. Now, for instance, in my own case, I came out of Tuskegee, I graduated high school there in 1928. And with excellent -- as a printer.
Uh huh.

Now after I came north, well, I went to school one year in a one year college at Talledega where I took a music major. But the disadvantage of the schooling at Tuskegee, I was not able to use it when I came north because I went to Detroit, and all my printing knowledge couldn't be used because I didn't belong to the union -- and the printers union was white only. Because I applied for jobs, like I was qualified to work on the Detroit News or the Detroit Free Press -- I could linotype at the government specified minimum of a professional linotype operator; but I couldn't get a job because of the segregated union.
But that was the fault of the system, though, not that of Booker T. Washington's teaching, because he had you prepared.
Yeah, I was prepared -- yeah, but the dead end was reached though, with the segregation in the unions -- and as you know, in our musicians union, in those
days, they were all segregated except maybe Local 5 in Detroit, I think, was never segregated -- and 802 in New York.

But you know, Chicago, we had 208 and 410, and right now in Boston, you have 9535 -- they're all amalgamated now, but oh, in those days, they were all segregated except New York, the big cities like New York and Detroit -- they were the only ones that weren't segregated.
Uh huh. You mentioned that when you left Tuskegee, you went to -- you just mentioned it.
Talladega.
Talladega, , that's right.
That's in Alabama, too.
Alabama. Then you went to Detroit -- so how did you get to Detroit? Had you started any music at all? We got to get in to that now.

Well, Detroit came in the picture because I had an aunt and an uncle living in Detroit -- my mother's ... one of her younger sisters who had -- one that was very close to her, one who had helped her in Austin, Texas, when I was born, this sister came out to Austin, Texas to help her with me and my brother so that my mother could go to work and teach. And she was sort of babysitting, taking care of me and my brother.
But when she later married and settled down in

Detroit, my mother used to visit her during our summer vacations in Tuskegee, and take me and my brother there -- and when we'd go to Detroit, I got a chance to hear jazz music, you know, on the high level of the big traveling bands, they would come through.

I remember Jimmy Noone band came over once from Chicago and played at the Greystone Ballroom. I heard regularly McKinney's Cotton Pickers Band every Monday night at the Greystone, and Fletcher Henderson's band came through with Coleman Hawkins and people like that in there -- and Tommy Ladnier, Kaiser Marshall.
Oh, Kaiser -- Kaiser's a Texan, too, you know.
Oh, he is? Kaiser Marshall is from Texas?
Yeah, he's from Texas.

So Horace Henderson had a really great band in those days, and Benny Carter, right out of school, want too, in Ohio, they formed this great band, and Rex Steele was in that band -- so I heard this kind of music in my summer vacations in Detroit, and when I go back to Alabama to school, they would -- that impression was just so strong, see. So that was really why Detroit was the town I settled in, and joined the union, tried to start a career after I had left school.
Uh huh. That's beautiful. Now
I'd like to digress just a minute. We've talked about Detroit and all, but when did you start piano? We hadn't discussed that.

That started at Tuskegee. I guess soon after we settled there, after my father brought my mother and Gus and me there. I started it with a wonderful woman named Mrs. Simms, who started many of the neighborhood children on piano. I guess my brother and I were probably seven and eight years old, respectively, when we started there, and of course, another thing with that school -- music study was just sort of taken for granted.

Oh, we would -- not only us, but all of the faculty that worked at Tuskegee, all the children studied music. I studied the piano, and shortly after that, I studied the violin and then later on in high school, I studied the oboe and the clarinet and worked in the marching band, played at the football games and that.
Right, right.

Traveled with the band, gave concerts on Sundays and march around the campus on Sunday mornings. And it was very common, it wasn't anything unusual at all -- all the kids studied music. It was just a normal part of the education.
Uh huh.
Oh, and all the people there
were very musical.
Well, when did you decide you thought you could kind of make it pretty good on the piano?

Oh, I don't know -- I lost interest a little bit in the piano when I heard the orchestra director, Maclo Williams, play the violin, as a young kid, you know -- I must have been about 10 or 11 then, and I suppose nothing would satisfy me but -- I asked my mother to get me a violin; I wanted to play the violin like Mr. Williams did, you see.
Uh huh.
And so he taught me -- but I played the violin all through high school, and still in college, I took up the viola because they needed a viola player.
Now what college was this?
Taladega.
Taladega.

Taladega College, yes. But after school, there wasn't enough drive, really, to stay with the violin, the oboe and the clarinet because of the actual practical reality of being able to work at the piano, see, and I had gotten into, after studying with Mrs. Simms and learning to read the piano, you know, you have to read the bass clef, treble clef, I was able to play in the dance orchestra
where you didn't have to be a virtuoso, but you could read a stock orchestration which is written -- that's all that was sufficient, to play for the dances.

And so that started, really, a career right there in Tuskegee, playing in the dance orchestra. But the classical foundation, and having learned to read, stood me in good stature. We had these stock orchestrations. Right. And then that branched on out to more advanced ear playing and improvising by ear, and then a professional career in jazz.
Sure. Can you in any way kind of recall any of the guys who were in the bands at that time?
At Tuskegee?
Yeah.

There were two fellows that I know made a profession of this who were sort of classmates, either one year before or after me -- one was Bernard Flood, a trumpet player who later worked with the Teddy Hill band in New York City.
Sure! Trumpet player.
Yeah, right.
Yeah, I knew him very well.
At the Savoy in New York.
Right.
And another was Thomas Stevenson,
the guy who pioneered with high notes on the trumpet with Jimmy Lunceford's band. He was a classmate of mine at Tuskegee.
Steve? Is that so?
Yes. We were all little kids togeher.
Oh, wow.
Yeah, in our band days under Captain Dry. Captain Dry was the bandmaster, and Macfo Williams as I said earlier, was the director of the chapel orchestra.
That's beautiful.

But I think that Floyd and Steve and myself are the only ones I can recall who, from Tuskegee, who did make it. Who stayed with it. Of course, from Alabama State, where I had some elementary school training, Erskin Hawkins became very famous.
Oh yeah; was he at Alabama State?
I'm sure he was there in those days.
Yeah, uh huh.

He might have been a little younger than me. He was probably there after I moved to Tuskegee. He was also in New York about the same time I did, when we both wound up in New York later on. But he's still very active, Erskin Hawkins -- he had many hit records years ago with the big bands.
Yes sir, he sure did. And that piano player -- who was that?
Oh, Avery Parish and his After Hours.
"After Hours, yeah! That's what it was.
Yeah, that piece is a classic.
And his Tuxedo Junction was really the one.
Yes, he originated that. Glenn Miller played it and was associated with it, but it was really an original Erskine Hawkins song.
That's right.
I think it was an original with the Erskine Hawkins band. They were a great, great group, right out of Alabama State.
Uh huh. So we know you've been at Tuskegee and then Talladega and all this. Now when did you first start to go and make gigs and do a little playing? What kind of groups did you go out with?

That would have been in Detroit late in the year, 1929. I went to college one year in Talladega, took a music major there under a very talented man named Tergee Debolis (phonetic) -- an excellent classical pianist and a master of harmony, and really knew how to teach the students the basic things that we really should know about music.
But that term began in the Fall of '28, and I

left in the Spring, at the end of that term, I guess around June of 1929, and that summer, went to Detroit and never went back to school. And joined the union in Detroit and just started club-dating around Detroit.
What was the local there in Detroit?
Number 5 .
Aha, Number 5 in Detroit.

Yeah. And I started doing club dates with people like Howard Bunce and an especially good friend of mine in those days, he was very helpful to me -- I don't know exactly how I met him, maybe it was through Howard Bunce, was Everett Barksdale, a guitarist. He's a very busy guitar player in Detroit in those days, and he put in a good word for me and my brother.
I guess we're getting to be around when I was about 17 years old in those days.
So that was about in 19 -- well, we're almost in the thirties now, right?
That's right.
And of course, as far as making a living in music, the stock market crashed right about that time, and we were just in time to hear the musicians talking about how good times had been.
Aha, me and you, we had the same finish.
Along with that stock market crash and the beginning of the Great Depression, the sound movie was invented, you know?
Yeah, Al Jolson came in.
Yeah, with The Jazz Singer.
The Jazz Singer, yeah.
And The Cold Diggers of Broadway, all that stuff, utilizing music on the screen.
And you stopped all the bands in the theatres.
Right, so we were hit doubly hard -- the overall economy and then our own profession, with the theatre musicians being thrown out of work. But we managed somehow, I guess.

Well, it was a tough survival. You and I were there, and we saw it -- because I remember, I was in Chicago, and I remember when Everett Barksdale came over to Chicago, and you eventually came to Chicago, too.
Uh huh, right.
Yeah, because I was instrumental in getting Everett the gig with Eddie South, and you played -- where did you play? Club DeLisa, and ...
I played with Eddie Mallory. Yeah.

When I came to Chicago --and I have to lead into that, but coming out of Detroit, I met Roy Eldridge in Detroit, he was based there as a young fellow in those days, and oh, let's see, Milt Buckner was, I think he might have -- well, I don't even know if he was born yet, but his older brother, Ted, was around.
Ted? Yes.

He was the lead alto player with Earl Walton's band at the Palais, one of the leading dance halls -- because the dance hall was a big outlet for musicians in those days, because everybody was dancing to our kind of music -- either jazz or some form of music, we called the sweet bands or the hot bands -- the jazz bands were the hot bands, so Billy Minor's band was flourishing, and as I said, McKinney's Cotton Pickers were going strong in Detroit.

But at my level and my brother's, the only thing we could do was being unknown teenagers, was to pick up club dates, and a man named Bob Krusett put us in quite a few gigs, local gigs around the area -- Bob Krusett was a saxophone player, and a man named Ben Shipp
Ben Shipp sure. I remember that name.
And we would play for weddings and whatever, you know, whatever the job was -- whether it
was a jazz job or not, you just played -- and sometimes it was a reading of stock orchestrations.
You didn't mention what your brother Gus played, too.

Oh, the trombone. Gus played trombone and piano, but his main instrument was trombone, and arranging -- Gus got into arranging, and was one of the most outstanding of us younger fellows in those days with his arranging.
Uh huh.

So a guy named Speed Webb came to town, to Detroit, and I guess this was still in 1929, late in the year, and he had just made a movie called On With the Show, where he was a bandleader in that, and the star of that was Ethel Waters.
Wow.

And the hit song from On With the Show, was the song, 'Am I Blue,' and so Speed Webb, since he had prominent spot as a bandleader in the movie, he wanted to tour and do personal appearances, so he picked up me and my brother, Gus, and Roy Eldridge from Detroit and took us down to his home town in Muncie, Indiana, and he got Vic Zach Dickenson away from the White band, or the West Helmet band, another road band; and we spent oh, a couple of weeks down there in Muncie rehearsing, and he got some other musicians
from Indiana, Reunald Jones from the Atlanta band; Reunald Jones finally wound up, some years ago, he was lead trumpet fo Basie, back about 20 years ago.
Yeah, but that was senior, now.
Oh yeah, I'm talking about senior. Jonesey we called him.
Sure, Jonesey.

So the Speed Webb band had Jonesey on one trumpet, Roy Eldridge on the other, Vic Dickenson on one trombone and my brother on the other trombone -- and that was the brass section, two trumpets and two trombones, until later on, we finally found an excellent trumpet player from Louisville who had modeled his mute playing after the great Joe Smith of those days, and played sweet solos in the mute --a guy named Steve Dunn. And that made the brass section.
By the way, do you remember who the drummer was?
Yeah, Scottie his name was, from Pennsylvania. I think Scottie was from Pittsburgh, but I can't think of his whole name, it was just Scottie.
Well, there's a guy, there's a star in California now that used to play with one of those bands. He's the star of one of the television shows, they played out of Cincinat with one of those bands.
A TV star?
Yes. A black guy.
In those days? Back in 1930-31?
Yes. He plays the guitar and the ukelele now on TV. Well, we'll get back to it.
Really? Well, I may think of it, yet, because there are so many of those bands that come to mind -- Wes Helms, as I already mentioned, Zach Whyte --
Zach Whyte's band -- that's it. same

Zach Whyte's band at that time. It was and my brother with Speed, Sy Oliver was with Zach Whyte, and Roy and Vic and I -- Zach had a great pianist, Herman Chittison -- and Quentin Jackson, everyone knows as 'Butter', was a trombone player with Zach. (End of side 1)
Right. Ohio was good territory for those kinds of bands.
In those days, we'd base ourselves, we did a great amount of work around the Cincinnati area.
The Sterling Hotel!
Right. The Sterling Hotel was like home to us, and the first time I saw those giant rats, as big as cats and dogs --
Yeah, they even had a special name.
Jerry!
Jerry! Right. I just wanted to mention that on the tape because people won't believe it.
Oh, yes. Milt, we would go on the
road and go out for a few weeks, and we'd come back and Jerry was still living in the hotel, just like everyone else.
Sure. And he'd walk down the steps right on by you.
Yeah, right.
People don't really believe that when you tell them that today.
The Sterling was right down there by the Ohio River, and they were as big as one of those giant river rats that people just have to see one before they die, they have to see what they look like.
That's right. He used to kill cats.
Oh yeah.
He 'd kill cats for fun. Do you remember where we ate in ...
In Cincinnati, we ate at Uncle Henry's.
Uncle Henry's, yeah.

Right, and it was 35¢ for dinner, and we used to call it pitch till you win. You ate as much as you could for 35¢. Can you imagine some of our friends now? If you would turn them loose at Uncle Henry's? They'd put him out of business in two days, wouldn't they?
That's right. We got a couple of them here, if we can recall their names. There was Chu Berry and Benny Carter -- very big eaters.
Benny's slowed down now, but yeah, I know what you mean. There you go.

Yeah. And I remember one time we were sitting there eating Chu Berry, and Benny Carter, and Uncle Henry was charging us 35 or 50¢, pitch till you win, and they ate so much, that when they got through, poor Henry gave them their 50¢ back and said don't come back here no more, son!
Oh yeah!
That's beautiful.

Yeah, those days are something, because the Depression was on and we had very little money -- many jobs we would play, in the Speed Webb band -- and I guess Speed was probably robbing us blind, I don't know, but I would hate to accuse him of that, but sometimes we would only get a dollar and a half for playing a dance, if it was a nice piece and the promoter would run away with the money --
Well, if we got $3, that was a good night.
A good night, right. But we sure had a good time, because playing the job wasn't enough for us. That was just the begining, though. After the job,
we would form a jam session, and each time we would find a piano or a little bar, speakeasy bar or someplace, and we could play until daylight if necessary, until the bus leaves for the next town.
Of course, one of the great spearheads of the jam sessions was Roy Eldridge -- he just loved to play, and find these trumpet players and blast them out in these different towns.
There's never enough said about Roy. He was a pioneer.
Oh, right. Roy Eldridge is one of the giants -- after Armstrong, I'd say.
Giants. That's right.
Absolutely.
He came through Milwaukee, Chicago, the whole area, man. Roy Eldridge.
He had that pure jazz feeling in his trumpet.
Oh, absolutely.
The essence of the jazz rhythm, just like in Armstrong, is in Roy.
Sure is nice to hear Dizzy say that, too.
Oh, Dizzy did? Uh huh.
Yeah, nice to hear that.
Well, Dizzy, I'm sure, as a young fellow -- he recognized that in Roy, too.
That's right. Absolutely.

And that's still there, too; I hear it once in awhile. It's real, like Armstrong, it's not to be confused with any music of other countries. It's American jazz, purely, that comes out of that trumpet.

Sure. And you know, one thing that most people don't really know, if it's possible for you to talk about, Teddy -- is being in black bands in that era before 1954, with the segregation thing. How we survived without animosity and without anger in the places where we had to stay and the places we had to eat.
Uh huh.
Now all over America, every black musician knew where to go to eat--- in every band would have to eat in places like Uncle Henry's in Cincinnati, do you remember Mom Sutton's in Atlanta, Georgia?
Uh huh.
Mother Hadlows's in Philadelphia -- you remember these places?
Mother's Lunch in Boston?
Right, Mother's Lunch in Boston.
Of course in the cities, though, you'd have a whole Negro community, like in Detroit, all up and down Hastings or St. Antoine Street or on the west side around Milford

and Westwood. That area was loaded with little Negro restaurants, where we would risk getting refused in white restaurants in those days -- hotels and restaurants when we traveled, so the best bet was just to go to the ghetto district where we knew the hotel situation, or rooming house or restaurant to eat or sleep.
Yeah. The Palm Leaf Hotel in Birmingham.
Oh? I missed that one!
You missed that one?
Uh huh.
Well, there were so many. It was a special life for us, and yet we survived it. We had to get rooms --
Like in Indianapolis, in the Negro ghetto district, the rooming facilities and food --
And so we knew that in each town so we could take care of ourselves.
Yeah, right. So when did you get to Chicago?

Well, after the Speed Webb band, something happened in Toledo, Ohio, and I got an offer from Milt Senior -- Milt Senior was one of the alto players with the McKinney's Cotton Pickers band in Detroit, and he left the band, and went home to Toledo and had his own little group at the Chateau de France Roadhouse, in those days -- Eckland State House
in the suburbs of Toledo, and his pianist was Art Tatum.

Well, Art got a job with WSPD Radio, and this is still about 1930 now, I guess, we're getting to -- and Art had played a half-hour solo every day of the week at five o'clock in the afternoon, and he did that and did it rather than play in little teeny small bands.

So Milt contacted me with the Speed Webb Band, and so I left Speed's band to join Milt Senior in Toledo, because it was steady, no road, and just like month in and month out, one job in one place, and location was right, and it was right for me.
Yeah, the location.
Great, that's beautiful.

And also, that was one of the best moves I ever made because I struck up a friendship with Art Tatum, because even though Art was only playing five o'clock in the afternoon, and a half hour a day on the radio, he loved to play -- he could play for 12 hours a day, and every night after I finished with Milt, I'd get together with Art, and we'd go to the after hour places, and different peoples homes, and friends of ours who had a piano, and the two of us, and visiting pianists would play until oh, nine o'clock in the morning, or noon -- as long as we could stay up and physically play the piano, we would take turns, and that was a very important point in my life, because Art

Tatum was a tremendous influence on me as a jazz pianist, because back in school, I had had the recordings of Earl Hines and the early Fats Waller solos, 'A Handful Of Keys' -- Fats Waller was doing the solos for Victor in the late twenties, and Earl Hines had begun to record with Louis Armstrong and the Hot Five. 'West End Blues', and all those things he did at that time.
Oh, yeah, sure.
And I had all those records, and I had never met Fats or Earl at that time, but I had learned the solos from the record, and I had already molded what I was doing at that time.

And then when I heard Art, that was the third big influence -- I incorporated what I could pick up from Art, and Art would show me anything I asked him to -- he'd slow it right down, and let me stand behind his shoulder, and he would show me exactly what he did.
He was beautiful.
Oh yeah. He was wonderful to me.
And he really could see a little bit through his eyes, I used to play cards with him.
Uh huh.
And he used to -- he would put all the cards up to a bright light and he'd put all the cards up there and sort them and --
Yeah, about two inches from his
eyes, he could see what they were.
That's right, that's right.
And even though -- his piano playing was the piano playing of a blind man -- by touch and by ear, the sight was no good to play.
Right.
But he could see two inches from his eye, a deck of cards, and when he would play cards -- do you remember -- the grace with which he could shuffle a deck of cards?
That's right.
Just like a master card dealer. Didn't he?
Sure did.
Just like he could handle a piano, he could handle a deck of cards.
His dexterity was just beautiful. I worked in the Three Deuces with him. Just amazing.
In some ways, he was the most remarkable and phenomenal human being I had ever been around.
Right.
I had never met anyone, in certain ways, that super, special born ability that he had. He was a very unusual person.
That's right -- he had a great mind to prepare for everything.

I rememeber in the Three Deuces in Chicago, which was this little club in the basement, he would come down early and have the waiters set up the tables, because he didn't want anybody to lead him anyplace, and he would let the waiter set up the tables so that he would know the avenue from the stairs to the bandstand without anybody having to lead him.
And, do you remember - he walked with a little bounce?
Yes! Oh, that bounce when he first stood up. Yes sir.
Right.
Yeah, I forgot about that.
Yeah, these are things that I think most people don't remember about Art, that you should experience. So please go on ...

Yes sir -- many wonderful evenings and mornings and early mornings with Art in Toledo and some of his friends, and in one of the places where he used to like to play the piano so much, and they served beer -- beer was his specialty, ice cold beer in --
Was this Val's?
No, that's in Cleveland, I'm talking about Toledo now.
Oh, I see.
(Beer)
In a little saucepan, an aluminum saucepan is what they served it in, a little saucepan would hold about a pint of beer, or something.
Uh huh.

And in that little saucepan, the aluminum would come frosted, with that cold beer and the cold beer in that cold pan was just delicious, and we'd play the piano and drink that beer on hot summer evenings there in Toledo.
Another lady who you might know from the London House in Chicago -- Alberta, she later took care of the ladies room at the London House some years ago.
Oh yes! She was -- yes, I remember her, sure.
Well, she had an after hours club in Toledo and she had one of Art's favorite old upright pianos in her place, and Alberta's was one of our regular stops.
Uh huh. Even Lovejoy's Out in Los Angeles, in the thirties? I played at Lovejoys in California, they had an upright piano there. The guy, Lovejoy, he used to be a comedian or something in New York.
I do remember the name.
He had a little after hours bar on Central Avenue, in LA.
Uh huh. Of course, one of the most famous ones that Art really liked was the one in Cleveland, Val's.
Val's, right!

Because Val's was the place. Val's had that big old upright piano in there, and Art loved it. Every time he was in Cleveland, and all the piano players from miles around would come when they heard Art come to town, and one of the fellows who I believe got on to Art first and started catching on to the key of those harmonic before any of us records of Art was Lannie Scott.
Lannie Scott, right!
Yes, Lannie Scott in Cleveland began to understand a little bit of what Art was doing, because Art was a real pioneer -- no one was even thinking of notes like Art did in those days.
Right.
So much of it was just like out of the blue sky, where you could trace some roots in Fats and Earl, going back through the history of great players --
Yeah, it was like calculus.

Uh huh. So much of it began with Art, as far as I could tell, anyway. Of course he was a great stride player, because we could trace stride back to much older players, since stride had been mastered by James P. Johnson by the First World War, as James P. Johnson was just fantastic with that stride.
But that harmonic thing, why, no one was even
thinking in those terms, that's common with young players today. But in those days, Tatum invented that whole thing as far as I am able to ascertain.
Oh, I agree. I remember working with Everett Barksdale with Zutty Singleton with the Three Deuces, and Lee Collins and Cozy Cole's brother was a piano player.
Yea -- Teddy Cole.
Teddy, yeah.
Sure, I know him.

Yeah, and we worked at the Three Deuces in Zutty Singleton's band, quartet, and Art Tatum was a relief piano player, he played alone, but I had to come on for his finale, I had to come on because he played a fast tune, I had to come on and close him and take him off, see.

And he would go through these changes which I never caught. I had no way in the world of knowing where he was going, and I stood there like I was lost, and it was just amazing how far ahead of the times he was.
Uh huh.
That was at least 1935 when I joined Cab Calloway's band.
Uh huh. A lot of pianists ask me about that Tatum thing, and I say the best thing I know how to become like Tatum is just learn everything you know on all

12 keys, be able to become a master of transposition, because that's what he had -- he had that harmony thing under his fingers where he could -- you know, he used to play 'Tea for Two' and change the key every two bars.
It was involuntary.
And make it come right back home as evenly as a fine patchwork.
That's right.
Just phenomenal. I still can't get over Tatum; I don't think there's been a phenomenon like him since.
Never, never. The taste and the dignity of that guy.

The touch, too. For a person who learned the harmonic system -- when you hear them play, the finesse of the touch is not there like Tatum had. Tatum's name was written on his touch and the other things all working together there.
Yeah. I remember a dear friend of yours and mine, Ben Webster -- who always used to say to me, 'I'd get up every morning, and to get my life started, I play a Tatum record.'

Sure. I found him to be a tremendous stimulus to me, because if I never heard Tatum I would never have dreamed that music could sound like that; I had no conception that music could be like that. But when I hear a Tatum record,

it opened a whole door to another world that had such possibilities. And he inspired me. A lot of players I met said they were going to be a piano player, but when they heard Art Tatum, they quit. I don't understand that -- because he made me want to play the piano.

But that's because, Teddy, you're an academic. You come through this thing and everything is cut and dry; I mean, you are now a senior citizen or a senior Senator of our American jazz music, and you did it -- you really added class and dignity to jazz. And this is what has been lacking -- perhaps all of our behaviors as jazz musicians down through history have been thought of as people like second-class citizens, but you never did. Your playing was accepted academically by the classical musicians. They said, this man is playing the piano!

Well, part of it was from my father and my mother and family -- and that environment at Tuskegee, all those teachers. They were well aware of the picture of the Negro in the white world as a clown, a buffoon, an illiterate happy person who jammed all day, but if people could see the environment of Taladega or Mo rehouse or know people like my father, Moten and those faculty people and the people around Taladega -- the people who are far removed away from the stereo type of the happy show biz, entertainer type of Negro.
Yeah.

But people are just as serious in those schools as you would find in Harvard, Yale or any of those schools, and the doctors there and the people in the professions have no stereotype racial characteristics at all.

But the other type was publicized because the show people equate us with the established white world more than in the other categories, because the show people had white audiences, and the known behavior of the Negro was a clown or buffoon, and not a serious artist.
Right.
Except I think maybe years ago with the singers, people like Roland Hays. Did you ever hear that name? A very dignified man and successful. Paul Robeson, Marian Anderson ...

Even the man that man that was with Anton Dvořák, that was in Ohio; great singer*---that was Anton Dvorak who wrote the New World Symphony. [Ed. note- Harry T. Burleigh, one of Dvorak's students, was born in Erie, Pennsylvania].
Uh huh.

That was dignity! But you as you say, with voice. were the first one musically, as far as I was concerned, and I've been watching you as long as you've been watching me, and I've seen your dignity -- and you're the first black musician that I've seen receive the dignity of a classical artist, the same respect that I would see for one of the great white musicians. And you did that, and you just brought it into a whole new different world. I don't now how it happened, but you did it.

Well, a lot of the exposure, I think, came from the Goodman, the spotlight thing was on the Goodman Trio because we were the first interracial organization in this country - we were 10 years before the sporting world, when the Goodman Trio came out of a recording studio, for years where there had been many mixed bands in the recording studio for years, but nobody played it live.
until the Goodman Trio was formed at the Congress Hotel in Chicago in 1936, when we played -- and the public spotlight was really on me, and Krupa and them.
But you were the first.

Yeah. We had a tremendous, big audience watching this new thing of racial mixing on an equal basis. Because before that, the racial mixing would be like Ted Lewis doing "Me and My Shadow" -- he would prance around the stage signing "Me and My Shadow" and the little negro boy would be following him and imitating every motion and be the shadow.
Right.
That category of appearing was widely known. But in a lot of states and cities, it was illegal for the two races to be on the stage at the same time.
Right.
There were a lot of states like that.
But there must have been somebody or someone that had seen -- well, you are the one who can do this, you are the one that can pull this off.

Well, the credit for that thing is -- and we're jumping a little bit ahead of our story, but this is very important and we can go back to the story. -- John Hammond has to have all the credit for that because he was the driving force behind the scenes of forming that Goodman Trio and putting me on an equal basis with Krupa in public -- away from the recording studio. But in public, right out in the open, he pushed and pressured Goodman to add me on as a regular member of the band, because Goodman and I had made many records in the studio; the Goodman Trio was born in the studio as far back as 1934, before Goodman was ever a bandleader, you know?
Uh huh.

And I had played on records organized by Red Norvo; I made a lot of records with Krupa, with little groups^ Jack Teagarden and Charlie Teagarden and you probably did, too, all the mixed bands in those days did.
Right, right.
Eddie Lang, Even back in the twenties, used to record with Lonnie Johnson and all those great jazz groups*-- they were racially mixed in those days.
Right.
(Ed. note- Lang recorded with Johnson in 1928-29 as "Blind Willie Dunn".)
As a matter of fact, the Chocolate Dandies under Benny Carter -- two of the Chocolate Dandies were white when I did it -- Max Kaminsky and Floyd O'Brien were two of the white Chocolate Dandies.
But that was in the studio, now.
But you were the first --
But John Hammond did that.
Yeah, he was tremendous; he did so much for that.

See, he could do that -- he had enough power and know how. He was a very smart man, you know, and jumping forward a little bit, when the color line was broken with the staff radio musicians, you know, John Hammond called on the phone the President of the corporation and said to mix up the band and that he wanted a mixed band in the studio, so they did it. And the NAACP was having rallies in Madison Square Garden and marching up and down the street, and nothing was happening. Here John Hammond gets on the phone, and breaks the color line in studio musicians -- Specs Powell, and I think you were there, and Cozy Cole, right.
Sure, Cozy and me ...

And he did the same thing in 1936 with the Goodman Trio. And Goodman went along with it, you know, and a lot of those people at MCA were telling Goodman, you're a young man coming up and you're a great clarinet player and you start this racial mix and you're gonna stop

your career before you ever get started.
But it just so happened it was the other way around. Hammond was right. Goodman became one of the most successful musicians financially in the business because of the race thing. The tremendous spotlight of pioneering. And then after that, everybody began mixing -- Billie Holiday joined Artie Shaw's band and Charlie Shavers joined Tommy Dorsey.
Well, we're jumping the guns here a bit -- I want to get you out of Chicago now. I remember, because I knew you in Chicago.

Oh, back to the story. Toledo. I was with Milt Senior there, when Art left to do the radio job, and a man named Ben Martin came through Chicago and heard us playing at the Chateau de France. Now we had a very soft little band, we didn't have a drummer in the band, and on clarinet, Milt played clarinet always on the low register.
Milt who?
Milt Senior.
Oh, okay.

And then Melvin Bowles was the bass player, and he was a bass player from Speed Webb - he also joined Milt Senior from the Speed Webb beside me. And we had a wonderful guitar player who sang -- Lester, he was a local player there in Toledo. His first name was
Lester, I can't think of his last name.
Uh huh.

But then Martin came to Toledo and had dinner at this place, and on his way from New York to Chicago -- he was on his way to Chicago to open a new club called the Gold Coast Club, and he heard our little band in Toledo, and he fell in love, and he thought it'd be just the music he wanted in his new club, so he offered Milt Senior enough money to take our band away from the Chateau de France, and we came to Chicago to play at the new Gold Coast Club which was at 19 East Ceadar Street on the north side, an old private building, private house, about five floors taken over for nightclub, restaurant, gambling, and it was quite a thing. One of the most elaborate places that's ever been built.
And what year was that?
That's right.

But you only see things like that in movies any more -- in movie nightclubs. But this place was the actual thing with a membership of about $500 in those days, private membership. -- members could come and drink and see a show, eat and gamble.
And you were in this band.
Yeah.
Ben Webster's. Who all was in that

And a drummer was added -- he got out of Detroit Freddie Bryant from Detroit. But Freddie dropped out, but he did get to do a little work with Basie, I think, during the forties or so. Sometime or other, he was with Basie. But it was still the intact band from Toledo. Milt Senior's band.
Well, did you work with Papa Bouchet's band at the Villa DeNice?

Yes, but that was later -- after the Gold Coast job folded, then I joined Eddie Mallory's band and that's where I worked with Budd Johnson and Keg Johnson. But my brother and I split up ways then, because when I went with Milt Senior, he stayed on with the Speed Webb band, so by the time I got to Chicago, I was in Toledo, I was on my own, away from Gus. Since we left school together, we had been together until that period in Toledo.

But in Chicago, it was still a spit away from the Milt Senior band to play with Eddie Mallory, an excellent lead trumpet player.
Lead trumpet player.
And we had a good band, too.
What was that guitar player's name? I see it all the time, and now he's a dear friend of mine.
Les Corley.
Les Corley!
Yeah. And also at Buchet's was the first nightclub appearance of the famous fan dancer, Sally Rand -- we played her first nightclub act.
Is that so?
Uh huh. And she later became very famous at the World's Fair there.
Tell us about that. That was in Chicago -- the Villa DeNice.

Yes, it was like fairyland out there in the suburbs of Chicago. They had an artiifical lake and a lagoon, and little streams flowing in the back with gondoliers singing, just like in Venice, Italy. And the show was all European acts -- like adaggio dancers and South American acts and European type acts. The singers were all clasically oriented; they would do -- I remember one wonderful tenor, an Italian tenor, he would do bits from 'La Tasca', the opera, you know, little arias andthen he would do certain popular songs that were suitable for a classical voice -- I'll never forget how he used to sing 'Softly as the Morning Sunrise', the best I ever heard it sung.
The jazz musicians have just since discovered that song and improvised on it. But oh, the way he sang that piece was something. But those were the particular kinds of
acts that Buchet hired.

And you guys, you musicians -- you were academic musicians, black musicians, that could comply -- this was one of the few places where outside of the theatre, where a black musican was qualified to play, because true, he was qualified to play any kind of music.

Right, we were like studio musicians. We played good dance music, we played jazz numbers with jazz improvisation in them, and we read this music of these European acts, when we were playing pretty classical music.

I remember one act did -- performed a very famous classical thing, 'In A Persian Market,' or something like that -- I think it was by somebody like Rimsky-Korsakov or something, but you got to play it well for these European acts. So we had to do that, along with our own music and the popular dance music of the day, and you know -- in those days, we just discovered, we were so crazy about the new writers, Rogers and Hart, and we played 'Dancing on the Ceiling.' and 'You Took Advantage Of Me.'
Oh yeah; that was a beautiful song.
And they wrote some lovely songs.
I was down south during that period.
Yeah. What was the name of that club that you and Eddie ...
The Rubyat Club!

The Ruby at Club, with Zinky Cohn on the piano. Oh, you guys -- I used to hear you on the radio, and Zinky was -- well, I had heard Zinky, but he came to Detroit once with Jimmy Noon's band, and I never heard of him, and I was just knocked out by the way Zinky played the piano.
Well, he was the same sound like --
Right, he was very much influenced by Earl. Yes
Trumpet with octaves.
But he was using a lot more finger arpeggios than Earl, but the basic influence of tha jazz attack was Earl's, there's no doubt. And he was very skillful with it, too.
Yes.
A number of those pianists who were so much influenced by Earl -- one of them was Cass Simpson.
Oh, Cass! [Ed. Note- Cassino]
I was crazy about his playing.
Oh, I loved him -- I worked with him when Louis Armstrong left the group north, I worked with him and Jabbo Smith.
Oh, yes.
But unfortunately, he was sick and he died in an insane asylum.
Yes, I heard that.
But he was a fabulous player.

Yes. Cass was on the radio, some places his own little group, his own band was broadcasting every night in Chicago some place, and they had a wonderful pickup on the piano, you could hear every note he played.
Right.

And of course, Earl was on every night at midnight from the Grand Terrace in those days, in the thirties. He's come on there with "Deep Forest," his theme song. Reginald Forsythe wrote that. Reginald Forsythe, he's a black man.

So we were talking about Chicago and the Grand Terrace, and that was when Earl Hines was in the Grand Terrace with that great band he had with Billie Franklin and all those guys, Cecil Erwin and Quinn Wilson. when I had
No, he Quinn was there. And George Dixon, Walter Fuller on drums. (Ed. note- Fuller on trumpet)
Remember that little huchback, the trumpet player, Mitch?
Hum ... I don't remember him.
He was one of the first trumpet players I remember there.
Cecil Erwin was on tenor, as you mentioned, and Omer Simeon was lead alto, and what a band that was. And then Jimmy Mundy came in later.
Dixie land banjo he played.
Right.
And they had a terrible accident in which Cecil Erwin got killed out there.
That's right.
I think that was when Budd Johnson joined the band.

Da, da, da.
Yes, uh huh.
And he said to me, 'Glad you're here, you're sounding good!'

Oh. A very talented lady.

time, and she had an excellent saxophone player, I can't remember his name, and Earl Hines' old girlfriend, Katherine Perry --

Yes, in Chicago.
Oh, that's marvelous.

'Some Other Spring,' da da da da ..
