And Carmen McRae recorded it, Billie Holiday recorded it, and many instrumentalists have done it.
Is Irene still around?
No, Irene passed away recently, in the last -- I think it was this past year, in '79.
Is that so?

See, we broke up -- Irene and I separated in the middle thirties, and she remarried a man named Kitchens in Cleveland, and stayed together, as far as I know, all through the years, and she just passed away recently, in the past year.
Oh, that's too bad.
But Irene and I never had any children.
Yeah, I remember that.
So you met Irene in Chicago, and you mentioned that you worked out there at this club in Chicago --
Yeah, I would sit in and she was there, she had a little band there. But in the mean time, I can't remember the exact sequence of all these things, but

back to the Armstrong -- working with Louis Armstrong, I think that'd be about the time that Irene and I got married, when I was with Louis Armstrong's band, and most of the work with Armstrong was on the road.
Uh huh.

We went down -- we toured down in Texas, in Arkansas, Oklahoma and Nebraska, Louisiana, Mississippi -- and Indiana. That whole area south and west of Chicago. And let's see, I got in contact with Charlie Beale.
Oh yes, Chuck.

Chuck Beale was playing piano around Chicago, too, and Charlie Beale was playing with Jimmy Noone, and for some reason, Jimmy Noone and I swapped jobs, and I mean, Charlie Beale and I swapped jobs and it was okay with Jimmie and it was okay with Armstrong. So Charlie Beale went with Armstrong, and I went with Jimmie Noone; but Jimmie Noone was another one of my idols, too.
Oh, a great clarinet player.
Before I'd ever met him, you know, as I said, I heard him in Chicago, I knew his record, the way he played 'Sweet Lorraine', and of course Earl Hines used to play with him, too.
Right, and Zinky Cohn also, later.
That's when I first heard live, Jimmie Noone, when Zinky was the piano player. So it was a privilege

for me to work with Jimmie Noone, and that'd be the last band I worked with in Chicago, and then from the Jimmie Noone band, I went to New York to play for Benny Carter. Benny Carter came out to Chicago.

I remember that -- I remember that very well, that's where I came in, because you were out there and I had yet to meet you and Keg Johnson, who was my dear friend, one of the dearest friends I ever had in life, and I remember the fact that you were in New York to join Benny Carter, and it was the talk of Chicago -- Teddy Wilson is going to New York! You know, all the local musicians were saying, man, he finally made it!
Oh yeah. Keg, too.
He came later, though.
We tried to get Bud, in, too, because Kay and I, like I was like the third Johnson brother, because we did get each other gigs and look out for one another.
Well, Keg got me with Cab Calloway, that's how I got out of Chicago. How I got to New York, and he told -- Keg worked with Cab Calloway.
No, Keg was with Benny Carter.
Well, at first.
Right. When Keg later went with Cab, and then I went with Willie Bryant.
Yeah.
After Benny Carter.
Right, and Cab went to California to make a picture with Al Jolson, and Al Morgan, his great bas$ player ...
Oh yeah, I remember the band then.

And he stayed out in California to join Les Hite and Lionel Hampton. And Keg Johnson, and now you gone and Budd was out, and Keg was trying to get me out, and he said, well, if you're looking for a bas$ player you got to go through Chicago, get Milt -- and this was my entree.
You left in '33, right?
Yes.
It took '35, '36 before somebody sent for me.
Uh huh.
But we were all involved in this. So you came with -- how did Ben know about you?

Oh, let me see ... Benny Carter had heard about me from John Hammond. You see, if you had a good radio in New York in those days, you could hear Chicago, because see, when the Grand Terrace would broadcast, At midnight Chicago time, and when Earl would go on the Road, I would sub for Earl with the Eddie Moore band. I forgot to tell you about that.
Eddie Moore! Yeah.

Well, Clarence Moore was his name, but they called him Eddie Moore, and he had a sub band when Earl Hines was so famous in those days from his broadcast, he'd go on the road, and they got me to play because they knew I was sort of like a carbon copy of Earl on the piano. Because I sounded like Earl.
Uh huh.

And that attracted them, so they got me to play there, and John Hammond heard me on the radio, because the New York stations -- when it's one o'clock in New York, they went off the air -- at the same time, we were coming on the air in Chicago at midnight. So John Hammond heard me, and he was already a friend of Benny Carter in New York and told Benny Carter about me.

So Benny Carter came out with his friend, George Rich, who was one of the richest racketeers in Harlem in those days, a very unusual man, and a real jazz fan and crazy about Benny Carter -- and the two of them came out in Rich's new Cadillac, and Benny Carter came and heard me, you know, and he liked what I was doing and hired me and then he hired Keg.
That's right. Keg got me the gig a few weeks later.
Uh huh. So Irene and I packed up our stuff, and incidentally, another commentary on the times there, the economy of the time -- Jimmy Noone, I was playing
with him and making $25 a week --and Irene quit working after we got married, she didn't want to play any more so she just stayed home and we stayed with a lovely lady in a rooming house, Mrs. Ardor.
Ms. Ardor! Yeah. Keg was there.
Right, on 4607 South King. Keg and Budd South Parkway. stayed there--rented rooms from Mrs. Ardor on It's Martin Luther King Drive now, but it wasn't in those days.
Right, Martin Luther King Drive.

So I was making $25 a week and I was married to Irene and supporting the two of us and living at Mrs. Ardor's -- and I was buying an old Buick, I had -- this was 1933, and I had a 1930 Buick, and it cost me $325. So we put all our stuff, everything we had in the old Buick -- and it was only three years old, then, I guess, and drove it to New York, and I joined Benny Carter. We played at the Harlem Club and George Rich was so fond of Benny Carter, and he had all this money, he was so successful in the underworld business, that he bought the club so that Benny Carter would have a job -- because George Rich couldn't play a note at all, on any instrument, but he had a keen appreciation of jazz, and he liked -- Benny Carter was his favorite saxophone player, and he actually bought this club so that Benny Carter would have a place for his band to play.
And it lasted for awhile, and then Rich -- for

some reason, he lost the Harlem club, and then Benny Carter took the band and got a job at the Empire Ballroom, which was downtown at 51st and Broadway -- upstairs. And we played opposite the Red Hague, and they had two bands, you know, the standard procedure at the dancehall. Continuous music.
Uh huh.

And then that job, after awhile, when that job folded, Benny Carter gave up the band and I went with Willie Bryant, and Benny Carter went with Willie Bryant as musical director, so he put Willie Bryant's band in the shape that Benny Carter's band was, so Willie Bryant had done that, and he was doing a lot of network broadcasting with this band, an excellent band, and made quite a few Victor records, the Willie Bryant band.
And out of that, I began to play for an excellent group from Cincinnati that had come to New York called the Charioteers, a singing group.
Oh yeah! Specs Odum was the piano player for them.
No, I was the piano player for them.
You were? I'm thinking of another group, then.

Sure. Billie Williams. And these fellows had quite a variety of vocal arrangements, and were very busy with radio. We were on the radio five times a week; they had three days a week for commercial, for a vapor rub product,

cold remedies and things like that -- we were on NBC three days a week and two days a week on WOR, the mutual network, and I was playing for those guys, and also I was the intermission piano player at the Famous Door on 52nd Street -- the first of the jazz clubs, and it had gotten opened by a bunch of musicians; I think Lennie Hayton was one of them; a lot of musicians went together and bought this little place.
What was the name of it?
The Famous Door.
Oh yeah. Ralph Watkins. Was he....?

No, that was before Ralph. I'm going back to about 1934-35 now, and I was the house piano player there; I used to play solo there at intermissions, and Louie Prima was there for awhile and Bunny Berigan had a small group there with Joe Bushkin on piano, and Wingy Manone's little band was in there while the period I played with them -- I played intermissions, rather.

And then, from there, I got a call from Goodman -- Goodman had become a bandleader during 1935 and with a regular show sponsored by the National Biscuit Company, a three-hour radio program, and when that went off the air, he kept the band together, because the band was only organized for the radio, but he kept it together and they performed at the Billy Rose Music Hall in New York, and then he took the band on the road. And the backbone of the writing was Benny Carter and Fletcher Henderson in those days. That was the
original Goodman big band style. And the band toured the country and flopped all the way down the line and finally made a big hit in Los Angeles, at the Paramount Ballroom.

And then on their swing back east, they stopped at the Congress Hotel in Chicago for a long run, and they started having Sunday afternoon jazz concerts, and guests beside the Benny Goodman band playing the afternoon program, and they brought me out from New York from the Famous Door -- I took leave one Sunday afternoon, and that was when John Hammond got Goodman to hire me and keep me on, and I never did go back to the Famous Door.
That's wonderful.
I stayed with Goodman with the trio for a year.
What year was that now?
That was 1936.
Yeah.
And then later on, Lionel Hampton joined the small group as a quartet and that continued with me until 1939, and I left to form a big band of my own.

That's right -- now that's where I tie in with you -- in 1936, I came to New York to the Cotton Club with Cab Calloway, and you were with Goodman, and you had a contract to do a record with Billie Holiday.

Right, the Holiday session started, and John Hammond set those up with Brunswick Records in 1935, and then when Brunswick went out of business, it concentrated on bowling and billiard balls, the stock was sold to Columbia, and we continued right on with Columbia with Billie singing, these small all-star bands, and you did bass, and John Kirby did bass, and --
Right -- whoever was in town, eh?
Yeah, whoever was in town, yes.
Whoever was in town we would use.
We had a lot of Ellington's men on them.
Yep. I got some with Helen Humes; I got some with Charlie Christian; whoever was in town, you used them on bass, and was gracious that remembered me from Chicago and used me.

But when you started that big band, you called me and offered me a job, and I don't know if you remember that, Teddy, but you're such a beautiful human being, and I got to tell you this, man, and it's got to go down as a matter of record and when you called and said, 'Milt, I'd like to have you join us, because I'd been making records with you and like you so much,' and the salary wasn't going to be the same salary that I was making with Cab -- but of course, I couldn't take a cut, and I said thank you -- and you said to
me, and I shall never forget these words, you said, 'Milt, I tell you this, I'd like to have you -- but whoever I start with I'm gonna keep' and you got Al Hall and you kept him.
Uh huh.

And I can remember the respect I had for you, for being faithful -- and you've always done that. You didn't say if you got free later, I promise you the job -- and that has got to be highly respected.
Yeah, because we got to be like a close knit rhythm section, a family thing, everybody was friends.
Give me the names of those guys.

Well, Al Hall was on bas$, and then I heard J.C. Heard in Detroit and brought him to New York, on drums -- J.C. was a swinging little drummer, he was a teenager when he joined my band, and he had never played in a big band in his life, but he was playing with Bill Johnson's band at the Cozy Corner in Detroit, I think it was.
That's right -- the Cozy Corner!
On St. Antoine or Hastings, one of the streets.
And he was swinging, too. But he learned how to play in a big band with me, and he was a swinging drummer.
Uh huh, right.
Incidentally, he stumbled upon a lot
of the techniques that Jo Jones was pioneering in those days.
Right.
There was a similarity in their playing the different things -- Chick Webb and Big Sid and Cozy.
There was a difference. Right.
They had found a few little things, and some similarities, too.
Well, he graduated from your band to Cab's band later.
Yes, uh huh.
Because of that.
Well, my guitar player was one of the best that's ever been, Al Casey.
Oh, God, yes.

Yes, Al Casey is one of the greatest. Of course, in those days, all the players played like what Freddie Green does now, played time, you know, four swinging beats to a measure, and of course, Freddie Green has never been surpassed, but Al Casey was one of the great four-four guitar players, like Allen Reuss.
Uh huh, that's right.
But he had his own touch and his own stroke as to how to play that chord just so and make it swing. Didn't they?
Sure did. In the annals of black musicians, I don't think -- there was never a band like you had. Nobody was established as a star or a biggie except Ben.

Ben Webster, yeah. And Ben was to become much bigger, because after he left my band, he joined Duke Ellington, and that was when Ben's career went way up, working with Duke, and then after Duke, he was an international star until he died on his own.
That's right. And those records. It's just unfortunate that recording companies only pressed a certain amount of jazz records in those days.

They never had the cooperation by the men behind the scenes. John Hammond never liked the big bands, and he was my main backer, and with him not supporting it, it died a natural death. We made about 20 sides for Columbia, and Columbia has never reissued those 78's, or never reissued them on LP ; but the excellent LP's have been issued and bootlegged in Europe.
Right.
I have copies of two different Grade-A bootleg LP's from my big band, done in Europe, different country.
Is that right?
Yes sir, but Columbia has never done it.
That's so unfortunate.
Because they never had the cooperation. And see, another thing, the band wasn't there again, the typical black jazz band of the time.
Right, it was like you -- it had class and dignity.

Now I wouldn't put down that swing thing, because we were not long enough together to develop a good head, because see, you got to have those good head arrangements, that's the best jazz. Now Basie was wise in concentrating on head arrangements instead of making so much emphasis on written. See, I was concentrating on writing for me written arrangements, like Buster Harding and another guy named Danny Mendelson, I was doing a lot of it myself, I borrowed Edgar Sampson, he did quite a bit -- and we were trying to make written notes swing, like with Duke, like Duke Ellington had been doing.
Yeah.

And were lax on the good head arrangements which you need for crowd pleasing -- when you play a battle of music, it's the head arrangement that you could play for about 10 minutes and get the dancers going.
Uh huh.
Like Basie's 'One O'Clock Jump' and Chick Webb used to play -- no band could stand up to Chick Webb when he played Get Together.1)
Oh no, that's true.
That was the end of the dance!

But when they got through with that, there was just no more to be played. I'll never forget the battle of music between the Benny Goodman band and Chick Webb at the Savoy one year there, and even with Hampton and Wilson in the band, you know, the mixed racial thing, it didn't do any good; Chick blew us out of there. With 'Get Together.'1)
He'd just whip that out, wouldn't he?

And Gus would say don't feel bad because there's no band who could compete with Chick on that one. They said Duke could blow Chickout, he was the only one, that's what I heard, and I would have loved to have heard a battle of music with Duke and Chick -- because Duke could play those things, and come up with some of those long drawn out things and those great swinging solos. Cootie and Bubber Miley, Johnnie Hodges.
Oh yeah; every one of them could take 15 minutes alone.
Oh, sure they could.
Well, that was fantastic. That era.
It was a wonderful period, the thirties, wasn't it?
Yes sir. Now talking about that big band of yours, Teddy -- did we mention the personalities yet? We talked about some of them.

Rudy Powell was the lead alto, and third alto doubling on the baritone sax was Pete Clark, who had been with the Chick Webb before that, and on second tenor was George Irish from Boston, who was not a great soloist, but a great section man, and then Ben Webster on first tenor. And then in the brass section, I had Karl George on trumpet.
Yeah, mention something about him, because he was fabulous.

Yeah, he was a fabulous trumpet player, and I don't know what happened to Karl; I think after my band broke up, I think he went with Stan Kenton for awhile, and then I lost track of him. And then my other trumpet player that I was so proud of was Harold Baker, who --
Oh, Shorty Baker.

He was discovered by Don Redman in those days, and of course Shorty went on to become very famous playing for Duke, and unfortunately, he died a young man. But he had one of the most beautiful tones of that day on trumpet. And the lead parts that Harold played were

really classics.
And then the trombones, I had from Pittsburgh, Floyd Beatty -- we called him Stumpy, a little fellow, playing trombone.
He's still around New York.
He is? Stumpy still around?
Sure.

MR. WILSON: Well, Stumpy goes back to those days with the Zach White band, and he was with one of those bands. And then my other trombone player was -- and I'm very proud of him, Jake Wiley from Detroit. He was playing a technique on the trombone that is still in vogue to this day. He was one of the area players, being taught by a man in Detroit, Bobby Byrne's father -- Bobby Byrne, a white trombone player, was creating quite a bit of comment among musicians in New York in those days, he had organized his band and used the slide for jazz.
Yeah. But Bobby Byrne's father, he had a reputation for being a most generous and most democratic man, even more than his son.
Uh huh.
In that he helped so many great musicians, black and white.
Yeah. Well, Jake Wiley was one of the people Bobby's father helped. And we mentioned JC on the drums and Al Casey was on the guitar, and Al Hall on bass.
Yeah.

And then, my right arm in that band was another piano player -- Buster Harding. Buster Harding was my main man for arranging, and a lot of times he'd play piano in the band and I'd stand up in front, because the agents figured that in those days they always would have a front man in the band, and even Chick Webb -- Chick Webb Bardu Ali would play the theatres, he would hire to stand in front of the band with a stick so the agents felt that unless I was being featured on the piano and was playing in the rhythm section, I would stand in front, and then Buster would take over on the piano, so whenever we could, we would actually have two piano instruments on the job, and our main job, which lasted so long, the Golden Gate Ballroom in Harlem, we did have the two pianos there.
What's the name of that ballroom?
The Golden Gate.
And how far was that from the Savoy?

One block down. It was in the old Cotton Club building. The Golden Gate Ballroom. Sometimes on a weekend, there would be five bands in there. But my big band, and Andy Kirk -- we were the house bands, and Andy Kirk had a wonderful band there, too. He had Mary Lou Williams on piano, and Don Byas was his featured tenor. He had

two good tenor players, Don Bias and Dick Wilson -- and he had one of my favorite lead trumpet players, Big Jim -- and I don't know Big Jim's last name, but he was one of the great trumpet players of all time.

Yeah. Jim ... I know his name because he works for the subway now, if he hasn't passed away, because my wife was a friend of his wife's. And they also had a John Williams, MaryLou Williams' husband, who was a baritone sax player.
That's right, John Williams was in that Andy Kirk band, and Floyd Smith was on the guitar.
Oh, a great guitarist. Thigpen on drums, Ed Thigpen's father.
And Ben on drums. Oh, Andy Kirk had a great band. I can't think of his trombone player's name, I think it was Russell Bowells, but Russell Bowells was with Jimmy Lunceford.
He was with Lunceford's band, yes he was.

But any way, Andy Kirk and me, we were the house bands at the Golden Gate, and on weekends, they would augment it; beside us, they would bring in sometimes two other bands, sometimes as many as three more bands.
Now what year was this?
That would be 1939-40.
Well, I was at the Cotton Club, because we used to come up there, you know, when we got
off, we'd come up there to hear you guys, because you had THE band.
Well, I think the Cotton Club had closed then.
We were at 48th and Broadway.
Oh, that's right -- the Cotton Club moved downtown.
We were downtown, right.
We were there when the old Cotton Club was in Harlem.

We moved downtown in 1936. And we used to get off, and you were a new innovation because you had offered me the job and I couldn't get the job because I was with Cab and we were doing pretty good, and now you branched out from Benny, and we want to see you do it. But I can't start with a beginning band when I'm already established with a band. And we would come up to hear you, and you had Ben Webster, who had been with Cab's band, and he was with Cab when I joined the band, and I would come to hear you and we would come up to hear you guys and this was the new band, this was the thing that we wanted to see happening.
Name a couple of the arrangements, Teddy, that you did. 'Sweet Lorraine' was one of them.
Yeah, that was one of my arrangements, 'Sweet Lorraine.'
Oh, I can sing those sax@phone parts, man.
And Ben Webster did an original for us, called '77', and that was just a number in the book and Rudy Powell did an excellent original for us called "Coconut Groove."
But I did a great many current pop tunes that came out, as they were brand new. (PAUSE IN TAPE)
Okay, go on.

I had an excellent arranger named Danny Mendelson, a young white fellow from Newark, and he did quite a few of the current pop tunes that came out in those days, and he studied quite a bit of orchestration and some of the sounds of the band was largely responsible to Danny Mendelson.
Oh, beautiful; I didn't know him.
He died a young fellow, unfortunately; so did Buster.
Oh, Buster Harding, yeah.
After my big band broke up, Buster did a great amount of writing for Basie.
He came to Cab Calloway, too, he did a lot of stuff for us.
Uh huh, yes. Buster was a very talented man.
Very talented.
And he was a swinging piano player, too.
He was out of Cleveland, wasn't he?
Buffalo.
Oh, was it Buffalo?
Yeah, he was from Buffalo.
And that big band of mine, finally, without the cooperation of the booking office, I couldn't pay the man and I had already invested all of my savings from working with Benny Goodman.
Benny, yes.

I had to finance the band myself, you know, get them the uniforms and the PA set to carry around on the road with us, and buying arrangements and the stands, and all the equipment you need to run a big band, I had done that myself rather than borrow money to pay it back. I could have borrowed money at exorbitant interest, like at 40% interest, but I had saved up money from Goodman to do it myself.
Uh huh.

But the money began to run out, and without the cooperation of MCA, the booking office, to book us in decent jobs and keep it going, the band began falling apart, and this way, the person -- when Ben left, Duke got Ben, and I got a good man in Ben's place, in Tab Smith. Now Tab was a great alto player who switched to tenor.
Oh yes, I know Tab. He was with Chick
Tab? I'm not sure. But Tab was on alto, but he came to my big band, and he did a good job sitting in Ben's chair playing all the solos that Ben had played and meeting the part.
And something happened -- Tab left and then I finally got a good man with a big sound named Bob Carroll.
Oh yeah, I know Bob Carroll.
Great big guy.
Oh, big. Great saxophone player.
Right. But then Bob got drafted in the army, and the Second World War was coming, you know, and this was about 1940 and they were put on the draft, and everybody went --

So I got offered, during that time, a job at the Cafe Society downtown, which was due to John Hammond's work again, because he never liked my big band, and so he offered me a job, a steady, year round job as a band leader at the Cafe Society, but I would have to take his men, his personnel.
Uh huh.
He wouldn't take the men out of my big band, he didn't like them -- but to his credit, he did offer us a good job.
He sure did.
And so I had been in debt and had lost all my money with the big bands, I took this job to
try and climb out of the debt that I owed and John Hammond offered me $100 a week in a permanent job and I knew that at least I'd have $100 a week and I could save a little money.
Sure.
I knew my car was paid for, and stuff like that.
And you always had a good car.
Yeah, a Cadillac.
Tell me about them cars, because you've been a car man all your life.

Yeah -- Cadillacs, LaSalles, and in those days before they used to make sports cars, and the old Big wheeling cars. Studebakers back in the old days. You could ride all over New York for a week on a gallon of gas! I remember I had a free wheeling Studebaker.

But anyway, I took the job at the Cafe Society and I did have a great little band there. I had Bill Coleman on trumpet, and Jimmy Hamilton on clarinet -- nobody had ever heard of Jimmy Hamilton in those days, before he went to Duke -- and then Benny Morton on trombone, which was hard to beat; I couldn't afford Benny Morton in my big band, and Al Hall went along with me, though, from my big band on the drums.
On bass.

On base, yeah -- and I had Yank Porter on drums. And I think J.C. might have gone with Cab along that period, but that was my little band in Cafe Society, and it began to change -- after awhile, Big Sid came in on drums in place of Yank Porter, and after Sid, I think Sid might have gone with the Armstrong All Stars or something there, and then J.C. came back with me, J.C. was in my small band.
But all through that period in the Cafe Society, which lasted four years, between the Uptown Cafe and the Downtown, the one in the Village.
The one downtown? I think I even did something with you in the downtown one, I can't remember where it was, maybe it was a day or something.

Yeah. Well, Benny Morton was the one musician straight through the whole period -- never changed trombones, and let's see, on clarinet, Jimmy Hamilton went with me, too, and then I was fortunate in getting Ed Hall, one of the greatest jazz clarinet players that ever lived.
Oh, that's right.
Ed Hall was with me to the end of my run with the Cafe Society, and on trumpet, after Bill Coleman went to Europe, then I got Joe Thomas came with me for awhile -- do you remember Joe Thomas?
Sure, Kansas City, saxophone player.
Not the saxophone player -- the trumpet player.
Oh, Joe Thomas, the trumpet player. Right.
Yeah, Joe was married to a very good singer, Babe Fay Matthews.
Babe Matthews, yes!

But Joe was a great trumpet player, too. Joe did some time with me during the Second World War, and then when Joe left, I forget why -- but I was fortunate enough to get Emmett Berry on trumpet. And he's a swinging trumpet player. And I think that was the band, when I left, I let the band go, and Barney Josephson started getting on me because I didn't rehearse the band. We were a jazz band, but he felt he wasn't getting his money's worth unless we rehearsed, and we were playing for him from eight o'clock at night until four o'clock in the morning, and yet, he wanted us to come in there in the afternoons and rehearse and he'd applaud the music. And he wasn't even featuring the band -- we were there to play for the acts. The band would back up, the drummers would back up Hazel Scott or we'd back up singers like Lena Horne and play bits of music with the comedians like Zero Mostel, and we'd play for the dance, acts, the Crab Sisters, and we'd play the background music for Jimmy Savo and those people, but we weren't featured.
But Josephs didn't feel like he was getting his money's worth -- because we worked eight hours a night, plus we come in there after hours to rehearse. But I just refused to do it, see.

So then he was supposed to have fired me or something -- I forget what just happened. But coupled right with that, I got an offer to go back with Goodman to do his show, Seven Lively Arts. And that paid very well, certainly much more than the $100 that Joseph was paying me.
I think Cozy did that with you, didn't he? Cozy Cole?
No, Morey Feld was on the drums.
Oh, Morey Feld?
Yes, and Sid Weiss was on the bass.
Bass, yes, sure.
And Red Norvo on vibes.
Aha.

So I went with Benny for that show and it lasted over a year, I guess it was, about a year, because the feature stars in it on stage were Beatrice Lily and Bert Lahr, and it was quite a musical event because Stravinsky composed the music for the ballet duo of Alicia Markova and Anton Dolan -- they did a special two person dance, a pas de deux, with original music composed by Igor Stravinsky, and the overture to the second act was composed by
William Shuman who was then on the way to becoming the new young President of Juilliard, and now he's President of Lincoln Center.

And the chorale, the music, the popular music of the show was composed by Cole Porter, the chorale was under the conduction of Shaw, that famous choral conductor -- Bob Shaw I guess his name is. And he conducted the chorus in a gorgeous arrangement of 'Every Time We Say Goodbye,' acapella thing. So the show -- and Goodman's Quintet playing jazz. Billy Rose really loved music, and he surrounded himself with some of the best music that you could have at that time. All put together, it didn't mesh or blend as a show, but he did have -- he presented Benny Goodman and one show, Benny Goodman, Igor Stravinsky, and William Shuman and Cole Porter.
All together.
Yeah, all in the show. Americana.

And the top ballet dancers, Dolan and Markova, of that day -- and the director was a top man, Moss Hart. And the show, called Seven Lively Arts, played at the Ziegfeld Theatre, which Billy Rose owned -- he bought that theatre. And that lasted for quite awhile, and then I met William Shuman during rehearsals there, and we had a lot of serious talks, and he told me, he was gonna be the new President of Juilliard, and would I come up and start a jazz piano course when he became President, and I said I'd be glad to. And I did. And after
the show, I started in about 1945, I guess, and lasted for about 8 years -- and I taught the jazz piano in summer school.
Well, Dick Hyman was one of your students, wasn't he?

1980, Dune is 13, James is 14, Steven is 21, Steven will turn 22 next month, February 7th, Bill is 22, he turned 22 about November 6th, he's three months older than Steven. And Ted has turned 33, his birthday's May 30th. Dune's birthday is December 6th and James' is July 27th. And these five are all very precious to me. Everyone is a musician and the interesting thing about them all, they've all got perfect pitch and I don't. I have lousy pitch but all my children have perfect pitch.
That's amazing.

Dune, my little girl, plays alto saxophone, violin, and plays these instruments in the school ensemble groups. And she's been studying piano since she could just about walk. And she sings beautifully and also she studies tap, acrobatic, and a very talented ballet dancer. And with the dancing they've gone far enough to perform away from the school in some special events quite often.

And her brother James is 14, he's got a drum set and a French horn, and he's been playing the piano since he could walk, and studying piano, and he's now playing trumpet in the highschool marching-concert band and piano in the jazz band and he studies tap dancing and acrobatic dancing. And also performs with his sister occasionally. And Steven, as I mentioned, is at Berkeley College of Music.
I've heard Bill play some piano, I think.
Yeah.
Remember Michael's Club, once you brought him down with his group?
Uh-huh.
There's something you just shelled out that I didn't know before, I don't think we mentioned it in genealogy, one of your children is named for your older brother. You mentioned a brother Gus.

Uh-huh. James Augustus, that was my older brother. He was a junior, that was my father's name, James Augustus. I lost track -- I haven't heard from my brother 15 years now. I doubt if he's alive, but nobody in the family's heard from him. My mother died about 13 years ago and no one was able to get word to him of that and no one has heard from him.
Was he into music at all?
Yeah, he and I were together with the Webb (PHONETIC) Band when we were in Kansas --
Oh, this is the Gus you were talking about?

Yeah. He did quite a bit of arranging for the band, Roy was in the band, and Vic Dickinson, who's Reinald Elvin Jones in the trumpet section. Gus was a close friend of Sy Oliver. Sy Oliver in those days

used to arrange for -- played trumpet for Zach White's band and we were in the Speed Webb Band. We'd run into them very often on the road, stay in the same hotel, play, very often, battles of music. So Sy has always been a great fan of Gus for that arranging.
Sy's an Ohioan, too, he's out of --
Yeah, (inaudible) Owetha Jackson, Zach White, Roy and I were together, played with Speed Webb.

There was a comedian out in California now, used to be a drummer, what is his name? He was on television, I think I saw him on the show the other night, that used to play with Zach White. I think he's a comedian now.
I don't know who that would be. Now, our drummer --
Scat Man Crathers
I know that name, Scat Man Crathers
Yeah, he was with Oliver.
He was? That I didn't know.
We were talking about Coleman Hawkins before. Tell me something about you and -- you were talking about how he did that thing --

Yes, Coleman Hawkins was one of that little handful of very special, exceptionally talented people, Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter, Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Art Tatum, these few who are far superior to the others in their

work. You know, they have an extra touch of genius and talent and most of these people, you find, are very individual in a way. They have sort of found themselves, their own path in life, and they're not pushed by every wave of the popular that comes and goes through the years, pushed from one side to the other like so many talented people. These people find themselves young, and they're on a path and they know it and they're just going straight ahead in their own way.

Like Hawkins, that tremendous ability he has. He's very unique. I thought that Coleman -- I used to work with him a few times, actually on tour, on the road working with him daily and making records. And I was very much influenced by his recordings, too. I learned a lot from his records along with my piano idols. And Coleman had the grand gift, I think, all this knowledge he had, it was always at his disposal. Anytime he picked up his horn, all this vast knowledge could be utilized, which to me is not so easy. Very often I know some things that I should have played that I didn't play. And Coleman, this tremendous mind he had, I think the continuity he showed in "Body and Soul" record, where every note logically follows the one before it, shows he almost could remember what he played from the first note on and relate all the following notes to the preceding notes. It called for a great deal of concentration and a tremendous grasp of music itself, to do that.

That solo is very unique that way, in an improvisation. And he had his own path. Once in a serious, philosophic discussion he told me he did not believe in things that you plan and work hard to achieve. Even if you get them, they're no good, he said. And they're not as good as what you thought they were going to be, and all the things over your life, he said, that really mean anything, the things that really are good for you, really good for you, are things you had no inkling they were going to happen. They come out of the clear blue sky with no warning at all. And those are the things that count.
So basically, if he's right, there's no need of planning. Just go with nature.
That's fate, it really is.
Yeah, right. And maybe he's right, you know. He sounded serious, he was very serious when he told me that.
Did you know Bird much? Charlie?

Not too close. I've made several record dates with him and some jam sessions and jazz concerts. I remember once when I was down at WNEW, he came out a few times as guest with the house band, and they'd have some jazz sessions there.
I didn't have too many close talks with him, you know, like with Coleman or Benny Carter. Because Charlie
from out of Kansas City, you know, he came with Jay McShann and Gus Johnson and Gene Raney Randall, they came about 1940 or so to New York.
So I didn't know him as well as these fellows in New York, because I always had lived in New York after I came from Chicago in '33. I was completely out of touch with the Kansas City group.
Hey, you know --
Did you ever hear Charlie say anything seriously like that, like Coleman, his views on life?
His views, yes, he was a very serious person like that, too. Charlie used to come by, when I was with Cab Calloway, he'd come by the theater and just sit back-stage and talk very seriously.
Was he very religious?

No, it was more lyrical about the injustices and social things in the world. And then again, I would see him later, when he got involved in drugs and the whole scene, and he would just be out of it. But when he was together, he was a very serious talker. And of course I did -- not too many records, but I did a lot of jam sessions with him, always a joy.
But you know something, both you and I, we've read the books about the people that he come up with and all that, and you've really got to laugh at these books because they're
so different from the way we really saw him.
We lived it, yeah.
Yeah, I agree. And Billie Holiday, like, you know. And you said John Hammond got you to do these things, but some --
Yeah.
Some of the Charlie -- what were some of the (inaudible).

Billie Holliday was not a particular favorite singer of mine. I liked, in those days for jazz singing, Ella Fitzgerald and I liked Anna Robinson and for ballad singing, oh, I just fell in love with Baby White. I thought she -- she just charmed me when she sang, 'You're my Thrill.'
Yeah (inaudible).
That's the real magic of singing, Baby White had.
What was she like?

She had that lyrical sound and I used to have a little bit of that later on when I had my big band, I had a singer named Jean Eldridge that Duke Ellington had discovered. And these girls could sing a ballad with their voices clear, this crystal clear sound, and lyrical. It was our kind of singing. They'd tell you the story and yet the beautiful phrasing of this clear voice. I think Barbara
Streisand has a little of that. Sarah Vaughn, to me, is just --

Yeah, who could -- these people can sing with no improvisation. They're spellbinding, singing the straight melody. And that's what I found in Baby White. But John Hammond, he was -- he didn't hear anything in Baby White. He was crazy about Billie Holiday.

But I had just left Chicago, working with Louis Armstrong, you know, and to me Billie was like a girl doing a take-off on Armstrong. It was novel, no one else had thought to do it, no other girl singing whose sound (inaudible). Ella certainly wasn't. Ella was doing her own thing, strictly. So I found Ella much more attractive in her singing, than Billie.

John liked Billie and the public, and you can't write that off. Billie was a big success. One thing about Billie, she could sing -- she had a very strong gift in that she could sing five seconds and her name was written all over the music. You knew it was Billie Holiday and no one else. That is a great asset to anyone.
Character.

That individuality, yeah. Original style. Well, I don't think it was original, I think it was inspired too much by Armstrong. But it was -- in a girl, there was nothing like it. And of course the musicians got -- I was

more excited about the musicians we had on those dates than I was about Billie, because we had Johnny Hodges, whom I'd been idolizing for years; Benny Carter, Lester Young was on, Chu Berry, Bud Freeman did a lot of them. Benny Goodman was on clarinet on a lot of them, Ben Webster on tenor, Roy Eldridge, Charlie Shavers, Bobby Hackett and Doc Cheatham and Irving Randolph. We used to call him --
Miles? Mouse
Miles Randolph on trumpet, Jonah Jones.
John Kirby.
John Kirby on bass, Grachan Moncuré
and you on the bass a great deal.
Right.
They had Walter Page on a lot of the bass and on the drums, Cozy Cole and let's see, Joe Jones -- I think they did most of the drumming. Gene Krupa did a lot of it.
(Inaudible) some of Gene. Alan Ruase.

Yeah, Allen Reuss. And Harry James did some trumpet. Dave Barber did guitar, Al Casey, Alan Reuse as you say, Freddie Green, Al Casey. Then the very first session, it may have been or most successful one in a way, John Truhart was on guitar on that one. Benny Morton practically -- I don't think we ever had another trombone player, it was Benny Morton all the time.

You know, looking back on it and the history of the Billie Holiday recordings and all the different things she did with all those people like Eddie Heywood and Tony Scott, the record shows that your records were the most fabulous. And we talked about the -- I don't think anything ever topped "Miss Brown, To You," and "What a little the Moonlight Could Do," and what about those sessions. How'd you guys get that impossible sound?
I don't know. That session was never, never surpassed. It may have been equalled, but never surpassed.
I don't know that it was ever equalled.
"What a little the Moonlight Could Do," "Miss Brown, To You," "I Wished on the Moon," and --
John Kirby, yeah. Oh, Benny Goodman --
Yeah, some of the best playing he's ever done on "What a little the Moonlight Can Do."
Is he labeled on that as Benny Goodman or did he take another name?
No, they had a phony name, because he had his own contract with Victor
I see. Physically, what was this Baby White like? What did she look like physically? Little girl --
Chunky --
Like she reflected?
Yeah.
She was light-complected?

Yeah. Brown complexion, about the same shade as Billie Holiday. Not so broad a face as Billie. Billie was quite plump when she was young. Very plump. And Baby was much more streamlined or slim. And, oh, I could listen to Baby White sing all night. Super phrasing, yeah.

You mentioned Anne Robinson, which was a talented singer. I'm trying to create an impression. She was in some show called "New Faces" once, I remember. And she did quite a few of those things from Nat Cole, I think, like "Hit that Jive, Jack." She was on the hit side with that?
Yes, that was her style.
"Summertime", instead of singing, "Your Daddy is rich, your ma is good looking", she'd sing, "Your Daddy was a millionaire, your momma was a ______".
Right, that's her. Some of her lines.
She was -- not a pretty face, because she had marvelous big, like Martha Raye's, that type. But a fantastic body.
Oh, yes, Anne, oh -- and also when Anne was word scat singer she'd go through the motions of playing a trombone.
Right.
Yes, she might have been the forerunner of the style that -- like Anita O'Day, I think her name was,
touches of it in June Christie and Chris Connor, some of those.
That's beautiful.
Unfortunately she died young. I never heard a recording she ever made.

I remember when she was (inaudible) I remember doing one record date with her, one of my first record dates in New York, and she made me the leader. And I wish I could find it because she had (inaudible) had some good guys and I was just with Cab and hanging out with her, so she made me the leader of the date. I never know where to find it.

I'd like to just throw some names at you, try to rehash some of the names of people you've come up with and your feelings about them, maybe you can come up with some of the things about the great people you have known through the times.
Talk about Joe Keys, trumpet player, remember him?
Yes.
Used to be with Basie's band, first trumpet player. And you had a great trumpet player, you mentioned a couple, your trumpet section in your big band, who was that?
That was Hal Baker, Shorty Baker, he's called, from St. Louis, in my big band. And when he came to

me, he'd just finished with Don Redman's big band. Then I had one trumpet player from Detroit, Karl George.
Oh, yes, I used to --

He was really good, too. I lost track of him. I heard after my band broke up he went with Kenton for a while and then after that nobody knows what happened to him. And of course, Doc Cheatham later came with me when I had three trumpets, after he left Cab.

That's right.
That's kind of like the old Goodman brass section, Chris Griffin, Zig Elman and Harry James. The parts were divided up pretty equally, first parts.

I have -- thanks to your son, Teddy, I have a tape of most of those things you did in that era -- recorded. It's just precious to hear. They're timeless. They're timeless, they're like John Kirby's records.
Oh, yeah.
People listen all the time and nothing would make me think it wasn't done yesterday.

Every once in a while one of the jazz radios here in Boston, Ron Delaquez or Tony Ponama (PHONETICS) will play a John Kirby record, and I'm just amazed all over again how excellent that old group was.
Well, your big band --

It was just so good. It was so good I don't think, maybe, I appreciated really how good he was until -- but everything was pretty excellent in those days. Sometimes I hear Tommy Dorsey records and Jack Leonard was the singer before Frank Sinatra. And those guys, they were as professional as a symphony orchestra.
That's right.
Play some of those Axel Stordahl (PHONETIC) arrangements.
Standard of perfection.

The Goodman band when Toots was in there on lead alto. And Artie Shaw's band, at the ______, did the same technical perfection of symphony orchestras. A thing, real musicianship, which was part of the music. That attack -- when the whole band attacks the one man, the impact is much greater than it was sloppy. Tremendous impact without being loud, when everyone attacks precisely together. Like Toscanini used to get on NBC. When he'd bring that baton down, that whole orchestra hit one note. It would blow the hall apart, wouldn't it?
That's right. It'd simmer.
The attack was just tremendous. And all them bands had that. But they rehearsed. They rehearsed. Goodman, of course, got to be kind of a bad fellow because he

didn't spare anybody's feelings, you know. He switched the first parts, switched solos in a minute, right in front of everybody. You give him that part, you let him play that, you lay out, let him play, let it be.

See, Dorsey and the other guys, I think, had more tact. But they were equally after this precision, perfection, which a big jazz band must have. Because Duke was the first with it. You listen to the early, small Duke Ellington band, the band back there with Tricky Sam and the band of the early '30s with Cootie and Bubber Miley, that precision in those sections, they would attack like one man, too. Just the "Ring Them Bells" record. "Dirty Glide," some of that period of Duke, that absolute precision was there.
The old McKinney's Cottonpickers Band. You know, in a big jazz band, that precision is such a great help, if you can get it. It makes the music much more important, sound more significant, I think.
In your band, that saxophone section did it. I'll never forget those beautiful saxophone changes.

But you had the men, too. A lot of men were conscientious. They all were playing saxophone. When we came together they had different makes of instruments. All the brass players went to Bach instruments, Bach flugelhorns and Bach trombones. They did everything to get this ensemble we got. They didn't leave one stone unturned and they were

conscientious about it. Because Rudy Palmer, my lead alto, was very important to me then, teaching the other saxophone players the way to make a tone for section work, (inaudible) because he had studied this with a fine teacher and he got Ben -- they didn't play the same when they took their solos as when they played in the section, to get the blend of the horns. So my band was working on those sort of values. I'm very proud of, and oh, it was really a bitter pill when it had to go. We just couldn't keep our heads above water without the cooperation -- negative attitude of the booking office.

Then, too, John Hammond, he didn't believe in it. He could have kept us going but he didn't get behind Willard Alexander, the booking agents, to keep us busy. So they just used us like a football, selling us cheap and telling us they couldn't get no money for us. I couldn't hold the band together, the payrolls, you know. (Inaudible).

But he had all those big guys and let me just throw some of these names at you that we can kind of talk about. There's Keg Johnson, which was your friend and my friend. He was in "Tailspin", he was with Benny Carter. And did you do much for Tommy Dorsey? Jack Teagarden --
I made some records with Jack that went very well in those days. There's a Moonglow record under the

leadership of Benny Goodman. Pick-up band years ago before Goodman became a leader. Then made some pick-up records with another great trombone player, Red Norvo's leadership, Jack Jenney (PHONETIC). He was (inaudible).
Oh, yeah, great trombone player.

Oh, I did quite a few of those small band records. Then with Benny Carter, the Chocolate Dandy series, and, you know, Chu, and Ben Webster did some of those. The interesting thing, you know the Chocolate Dandies was supposed to be like an all Negro group, the chocolate color, dandy is sort of a citified slicker, well dressed, sharp guy.
Kind of pimp.
Yeah, right.
(Laughter.)
But now the Benny Carter's Chocolate Dandies have Floyd O'Brien in there and Max Kaminsky.
(Laughter.)

But that, again, was the mixed band in the studio. The public does not know what goes on, which, you know, we talked before about the Benny Goodman leadership, taking a mixed group out of the studio and putting it out on the band-stand, in public.
But a lot of those Chocolate Dandies were all mixed bands. I thought that was kind of humorous, you know, the name would be all chocolate-colored musicians and half of them
were white.
Did you know Big Green, the trombone player (inaudible)?
Yeah, I worked with Big Green a long time in Benny Carter's band. Yeah, he was a great sax and trombone player. Always hit those long notes for us, he was powerful.

Big Green was funny, too, You know, he always -- he drank very heavily. He drank on a system. He'd drink on the night -- on the job he'd drink a pint of whisky during the evening and he went to work every night with two and a half pints of whisky that he'd knock off during the three hours of the dance when we were working the Empire Ballroom. And any musician who asked him for a drink he'd say, "I just have enough for myself. I'll lend you some money so you can go buy yourself some but I can't give you any of this, I just have enough for myself."
(Laughter.)
Several musicians joking, talk was (inaudible).
Surely was. In fact (inaudible) used to say, "Drink hearty and stay with your party."
(Laughter.)
I'll tell you who turns that kind of stuff on nowadays is Harry Edison. You ever see Harry Edison tangle up with musicians, they get kidding around, ride each other.
Yeah, 'Seen better days on a farm,' he used to say, something like that. Yeah, Sweets is quite a character and a fantastic player.
Uh-huh.
(Simultaneous conversation, unintelligible).
Yeah, to me he's playing a lot more trumpet than ______ was when he came over to Basie's.
That's right. He's very happy these days.

Yeah, I work quite often with him at jazz festivals. Of course, recently up there in Colorado Springs, Gibson's party. And I did a record date I'm proud of called "Teddy Wilson's All Starts" for the Chiaroscuro label a couple years ago when he was on trumpet, and had Vic Dickinson on trombone and Bob Wilber on reeds. Bob, incidentally, did the little sketch arrangements this time. And Major Haley on bass and we had Oliver Jackson on drums. And we tried to do kind of like we did in the old days. We made three minute records, the guys stuck with eight bars, and 16. No extended solos, every tune was down to three minutes. We did the same format on this all-star date that we used to do back in the '30s.
That sounds good.
You know, back in those days they played eight bar solos and it's a masterpiece, you could be heard
around the world.
Sure (inaudible).
Yeah, they'll play you two hours. But, you know, the best solo Goodman ever made on record was the "Moonlight Can Do," it was only 16 bars.
He sure was blowing.
That's right. That was 16 bars.
Some of the bass players you played with in Benny Goodman's band, Harry Goodman, his brother was there?
Yes. The whole period I was with Goodman, Harry was the bass player, before I came in and after I left. And later, after I left, Annie Bernstein came in on bass. Great bass player.
Right. And Sid?

Sid Weiss. Oh, yes, I played with Sid Weiss, much later, after I rejoined Benny for the "Seven Lively Arts Show" and then after that did some dates on the road. And Sid Weiss was on bass with Red Norvo and Slam Stewart. Mike Bayer was in the sextet with Benny.

Well, when you and I just started getting into New York in the '30s, let's see, who were some of the great drummers? I think George Wettling was around and there was -- who was -- Kaiser Marshall (PHONETIC), did you --
I never worked much with Kaiser. I was

very fond of Kaiser's drumming. I heard him with Fletcher Henderson's band years before in Detroit, before we came to New York. And I liked also, very much, Walter Johnson. Walter Johnson was the best drummer I heard playing an open-top cymbal, big cymbal on top of the drum and just letting it ring behind the solos.

Walter Johnson David Thompson was doing that when he came to New York in 1934 or so, that open cymbal. See, Sid, Big Sid and Chick Webb and Gene Krupa, they weren't doing that. I don't believe they were playing that, just letting that cymbal ring like that, which became -- and then of course Joe Jones came with Basie. He made quite a little change in style. But what he did still didn't take away from the greatness of people like Gene Krupa and Cozy Cole and Big Sid. Big Sid was a great drummer, regardless of the way the styles changed, the big, broad way, everybody plays this way, everybody plays that way this year. Big Sid was ageless, pure music. I think he was Armstrong's favorite drummer, too.
He was. So tactile for a big man, he was a huge guy.
(Simultaneous conversation, unintelligible).
Oh, yeah, but he played. He played with me in my small band at Café Society for years. Just played brushes mostly all night. (Singsong)
Well, my mentor, of course, was Zootie,

because I came up with him in Chicago. He was the drummer in Chicago when I came up, and it was the Three Duces, he hired me in his band. And if you played with Zootie, that was a stamp of approval. If you got to play with Zootie --
Somewhere along the line I played with Zootie but I think it would have been always in jam sessions, or special jazz programs around New York. I don't believe in Chicago, maybe.
I see. Going back --
When I was with Louie, he had a drummer named Yank Porter.
Oh, yeah, I remember that.
An old timer, when I was with Louie, 1940. And later on, when I went to Cafe Society, Yack was my drummer in New York before Sid came in.
(Recording interruption.)
-- when I had the small band at Cafe Society. J. C. Heard had been my drummer in the big band.
Yeah, you mentioned J. C.
J. C. later came back to me at the Cafe Society, with the small band. I would between J. C. and Yank Porter. Big Sid was my drummer. So that was talent, Big Sid.
Well, getting back to these drummers, (inaudible) drummers even though we're changing cities. Back
in the '30s right here, talking about this, did you know Tuggy Tedley Hall (PHONETIC) out in Chicago, Tuggy Hall?
Yeah, I know the name very well.
Did you know Bill Webston --
Tubby, oh, yeah, Tubby Hall. And Bill Weston, yes.
Bill is in Honolulu now.
He was a good drummer, Bill.
Yes, yes.
I think he was Irene's favorite drummer. Was it Winton?
Bill Winston. He was Johnson's buddy. All them guys all carried those guns and pistols and rifles.
Oh, yeah, he was a gun nut.
He was a gun nut, too. Hobbyist, you know, took to carrying them around.
We mentioned Kaiser Marshall, Zootie, and Chick, did you do much with Chick?

Chick Webb? Oh, yes. When I was with Willy Bryant's band and playing opposite Chick in the Savoy, every set I'd just listen to that Chick Webb band. And the band played so simple but it sounded so good. And part of it was that rhythm section, with Chick on those drums and John Kirby on the bass. That band swung so good that anybody
had to play one note, anything in the place sounded good.
Tell me about that band!
That was a very special band, that Chick Webb band.
And you were with Willie Bryant, you say. Now, when did you go with Bryant, was that after you came to New York?

After Benny Carter, yeah. I came in to play with Benny Carter and after Benny got out of the band business, he let the big band go, I joined Willie Bryant. And later on, while I was with Willie, Benny Carter came on and Willie saw it as a musical director and put the band in first class shape and played lead alto, too, himself, in the band. Made some arrangements for Willie because Willie was getting to where he was going to be the young Cab Calloway in a way you know. Because in those days you always had somebody in front of the band, even though -- every band must have someone in front of it, even though he couldn't play. Like, you know, Chick, when he'd do the theaters, he'd have Bandy Ali in the front, with the baton. So that's what Willie was.

And that made a start. Cab (inaudible) for that thing.
That's right, he took the _______ s over, didn't he.

Yeah, became a great star just standing in front of a band. That was -- Willy was covering -- we were doing a lot of NBC broadcasts and the band was going on the road, drawing crowds, broadcasting from the Savoy. When Chick would not be in there.
I was just thinking, even though we're jumping back and forth in the '30s between Chicago and New York, did you have any escapades, any association with Erskine Tate out there in Chicago?
Yes, I worked for Erskine many times. Triangle Club, on the West Side, and then on other occasions with --
(Recording interruption.)
That knock on the door was your son Steven coming back in. So nice to see him again. (Inaudible) last night and this beautiful young man, a drummer, it's nice to see you.
We were talking about Erskine Tate there in Chicago.
Yeah, I played with Erskine, several club dates, I guess.
How'd you find him?
I enjoyed working for him. He was a very nice man. I never heard him play his violin, I think he told me that was his instrument. He fronted the band, but he sure was a good leader.
Great disciplinarian.
Yeah. He sure knew how he wanted the music to go, and he was really nice to musicians, too.
Yes, he was.
Yeah, very considerate sort of man. He never said anything sarcastic, never raised his voice to any of the guys in the band. You know, club dates, they weren't so perfect, you know.

I can remember clear back when I was 13 years old in Chicago, 1923, Chicago on a Sunday afternoon, everybody went to the Vendome, the black people in our community went to the Vendome Theater to see Erskine Tate's orchestra. Weatherford
J. Jimmy Bertrand,
So these were the ones that we followed. Of course, you later got to play with him.

Yeah.
To have an all-star soloist in a pit band like that.
They could read music and play classical
things. Eddie South, Charles Elgar, remember Charles Elgar?
Yes, uh-huh.
He was one of Eddie South's teachers. And, as you said, he had a great band.

Yeah, had that large band. When I came to Chicago he'd given up the band, I think he might have been an official of the union, then. Highly regarded by the musicians; they told me they had a lot of respect for that big band he had.
He was using strings in those days, too, I believe.
Right.
Rather unusual.
And there was another guy, Dave Peyton, did you --
Dave Peyton, yeah.
He was across the street at the Grand Theater, 31st and State, I believe.
And that reminds me of Tiny Parham, you remember him?
Oh, yes, a pianist.
You know why they called him Tiny?
He was big, wasn't he?
He was so big, right.
